newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algerian opposition leader urges Clinton to act. [CORRECTED 18:13 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Algerian opposition leader urges Clinton to act. [CORRECTED 18:13 GMT]

text.p: Algeria's main secular opposition leader, Hocine Ait Ahmed, called on U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday to appoint a special mediator to help end the whirlpool of violence in the North African country.

Speaking to journalists in Rome, Ait Ahmed said the surge of bloodshed pitting Islamist guerrillas against security forces had reached a point where Algeria risked degenerating into Somalia-style chaos, with the country in the hands of warlords.

He accused former colonial power France, which is close to the military-backed government, of responsibility for inaction on a political solution and for indifference to the plight of Algerians "as if we were sub-humans".

"We would like this wall of silence, this Berlin Wall being rebuilt on the frontiers of Algeria, to be broken," Ait Ahmed, leader of the Socialist Forces Front (FFS), said, adding Europe had made itself an accomplice to violence by silence.
"One of the initiatives we expect is that President Clinton takes a measure likely to help bring about peace. Why doesn't he appoint a mediator on Algeria.
"We believe that such an initiative in favour of a peace process will be likely to unblock the situation, the international situation," he said.

Algerian newspapers on Thursday said nearly two weeks of bombings and attacks by Islamist guerrillas had killed at least 160 people, the latest deaths in violence since 1992 when authorities cancelled a general election that Islamists were poised to win. (Corrects to add dropped words "and attacks".)

News reports speak of 60,000 deaths. Ait Ahmed put the toll at 100,000 and said the latest killings, since the Moslem holy month of Ramadan began on January 10, were a signal from the radical Armed Islamic Group (GIA) that it could not be crushed.
He accused President Liamine Zeroual of using the emergency to suppress democracy, creating a political void that would play into the hands of extremists.

"The current debate is either war or peace. The rest is secondary," he said. "Today, before the civil war reaches a point of no return, international opinion must realise that if this process continues we will be moving towards a Somalia in Algeria...the multiplication of warlords whether they be true Islamists or militiamen."

Ait Ahmed and other leaders of the Algerian opposition, including the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), issued a joint appeal to the government two years ago to engage in a national dialogue on democratic life in the country. The call was rejected.

Ait Ahmed, who was in Rome this week for a meeting of the Socialist International, said Islamist extremists had to be isolated but that no peace could come to Algeria unless Zeroual agreed to dialogue with political forces on democratisation.
"The only factor likely to bring about peace is international solidarity," he said.

"I believe Europe and the United States must take real steps in order to convince the Algerian government that there will be no complicity any more regarding human rights and the rights of self-determination of the Algerian people."
He said French policy was being dictated by a lobby of commercial interests in oil and gas producing Algeria.
"We believe that to a great extent France is responsible for this lack of solidarity," Ait Ahmed said.

"When we asked European governments, even the United States, to do something in order to pressure the Algerian government into peace and a political solution we were answered that France does not want it," he said.
